questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The hypothesis a research question implies
questions.learningObjective: state the specific claim a comparative research question licenses the team to test
questions.stem: A team wants to know whether a twenty-minute walk before the first lesson changes how much of that lesson students recall an hour later. Which statement is the hypothesis that question licenses?

options.text: Students assigned to a twenty-minute walk will recall more of the lesson than students assigned to an ordinary break of the same length
Walking before class affects how much of the lesson students recall
options.misconception: restates the research question itself and leaves the direction of the difference unstated

options.text: Recall is the outcome variable in a study of walking before class
options.misconception: names the variables in the design instead of stating the difference between them

options.text: Twenty minutes is the length of walk that improves recall
options.misconception: offers a dose recommendation that the two-group design cannot establish

questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a claim about the difference between measured values under a stated condition, and option A is the only one that fixes a direction, fixes an outcome and keeps the comparison honest by matching the break to the walk on length. Option B is the research question with the words rearranged, which leaves a reader unable to say what result would count against it. Option C is a piece of design vocabulary rather than a claim about the world, and option D is a dose recommendation that a two-group comparison cannot support, because nothing in the design varies the length of the walk.
questions.hint: Ask which statement tells a reader what result would count against the team's claim.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Null and alternative that exhaust the outcome space
questions.learningObjective: check that a hypothesis pair leaves no outcome unassigned
questions.stem: A team insists that its null and its alternative must divide the whole outcome space so that no possible result is left over. Which pair of statements does that?

options.text: Either the mean score of tutored students equals the benchmark, or it differs from the benchmark by some amount
Either the programme raises the mean score, or the programme lowers the mean score
options.misconception: leaves the case where the two are indistinguishable in neither branch

options.text: Either the programme raises the mean score by more than five points, or it raises it by five points or fewer
options.misconception: splits a single direction at an arbitrary cut-off instead of at no difference

options.text: Either the programme is effective, or the programme is ineffective
options.misconception: uses labels with no numerical boundary, so the split cannot be located in the data

questions.explanation: A hypothesis pair is complete only when every possible value of the quantity lands in one branch or the other, and pairing equality of the mean with inequality covers the whole line in one step. Option B quietly assumes the two groups must come out different, so a study finding no difference has reported a result that fits neither branch, which is the commonest way a null hypothesis is written wrongly. Option C draws the boundary at a five-point target rather than at no difference, and option D uses words whose boundary has never been set, so a reader cannot apply the pair to a number at all.
questions.hint: Ask what a study would report if the two groups came out identical.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a pooled-variance t test actually assumes
questions.learningObjective: identify which distributional assumption a two-sample t test rests on
questions.stem: A report compares two independent groups with a pooled-variance t test and defends the choice by saying the samples are large enough that the central limit theorem will repair any skew. Which statement is the accurate objection?

options.text: The approximation describes the sampling distribution of a mean, so it removes skew in the raw scores but says nothing about the two spreads being comparable
The central limit theorem only reaches full effect above thirty observations, so a larger sample would have removed the concern
options.misconception: treats a remembered rule of thumb as the condition the theorem actually requires

options.text: Skew in the raw scores invalidates a t test however large the samples grow, so the approximation never helps
options.misconception: overcorrects and denies an effect the large-sample approximation genuinely provides

options.text: Unequal spreads matter only when a sample is small, so the concern disappears once either group passes thirty
options.misconception: converts a diagnostic about spread into a rule about sample size

questions.explanation: The pooled-variance t test rests on two separate things: the mean of each group is roughly normal, or nearly so once the sample is large, and the two groups share a common spread so that one pooled standard deviation describes both. The central limit theorem speaks only to the first, so quoting it settles half the assumption and leaves the second untouched, and a large sample with wildly unequal spreads is exactly the case it cannot rescue. Options B and D both turn a spread question into a sample-size question, and option C denies the first half of the assumption rather than the second.
questions.hint: Count the assumptions the test needs before the sample size earns anything.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The distributional assumption behind a one-way analysis of variance
questions.learningObjective: state the normality assumption of a one-way analysis of variance in a checkable form
questions.stem: A one-way analysis of variance compares four conditions, and the methods section states the normality assumption. Which statement states it in the form that makes it checkable?

options.text: The values inside each condition should look like draws from a roughly normal distribution, so skew is inspected within groups
The four condition means should be spaced at roughly equal intervals, since the test compares them on a common scale
options.misconception: reads the test as demanding a pattern among the group means themselves

options.text: The pooled data set should be symmetric overall, since that is the only place normality can be assessed
options.misconception: checks the shape of the pooled sample rather than the shape inside each group

options.text: The four group sizes should be equal, since the test cannot be run on unequal numbers of observations
options.misconception: believes the test requires balanced group sizes rather than a spread assumption

questions.explanation: The normality assumption attaches to the values within each condition separately, so it is checked per group, and a data set can be symmetric overall while one small condition is badly skewed and pulls the pooled picture into shape. Option B describes a pattern among the means, which is a finding rather than an assumption. Option C is the check students most often perform because it is a single easy plot, and it is the one that can pass while a condition is unusable. Option D confuses the assumption with a design nicety, since the test runs happily on unequal groups as long as the within-group shape is reasonable.
questions.hint: Ask where in the data the assumption has to hold, not what the pooled picture looks like.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: When a rank-based test is the required choice
questions.learningObjective: select a nonparametric alternative and name the condition that forces it
questions.stem: Thirty patients rate pain on a 0 to 10 scale before and after a treatment, with many tied scores. Which choice is defensible, and what forces it?

options.text: A signed-rank test on the difference between each patient's two ratings, because those differences are ordinal with ties and no usable spread
A t test on the two sets of ratings, because the scale runs from zero to ten and so has a genuine zero
options.misconception: reads a labelled scale as a ratio scale and treats the labels as measurements

options.text: A rank test comparing the pre-treatment ratings with the post-treatment ratings directly, because ranking removes the skew
options.misconception: ranks the levels instead of the within-patient differences and so discards the pairing

options.text: A t test on the difference scores, because pairing removes the need for those differences to be roughly symmetric
options.misconception: names the t test's actual requirement and then uses it as though pairing supplied it

questions.explanation: A rank-based paired procedure works on the order of the within-patient differences rather than their size, so it is the right choice when the differences are ordinal with ties, which is exactly the situation the ratings create. Option B treats a numbered scale as though its zero were a true absence of pain. Option C ranks the two levels separately, which throws away the pairing that made the design efficient and lets between-patient differences swamp the change. Option D is the sharpest trap, because it correctly names that a t test needs symmetric differences and then credits the pairing with supplying that symmetry, which it does not.
questions.hint: Ask whether the numbers are measurements or only orderings, and whether the same person supplied both.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: One-sample against two-sample comparison
questions.learningObjective: name the design that a single group against a fixed benchmark supports
questions.stem: A team has one group of forty trainees, each with a score, and wants to know whether the group mean differs from a published benchmark of 60. Which description states the design the data support?

options.text: One-sample, because the fixed benchmark supplies no variability of its own to the estimate of the difference
Two-sample, because the benchmark counts as a second group and its published error must be folded in
options.misconception: promotes a fixed constant into a sampled comparison and invents an error term for it

options.text: Paired, because each trainee score can be matched to the benchmark value of 60
options.misconception: treats a shared constant as though it were a matched partner observation

options.text: Two-sample, because the forty trainees should be split at random into two groups to compare with the benchmark
options.misconception: creates a second comparison the question never asked about

questions.explanation: A one-sample comparison estimates the difference between the observed group mean and a number that is treated as known, so the only variability that enters the standard error comes from the forty trainees, and the interval narrows as they grow. Option B gives the benchmark a sampling error it cannot have, which makes the comparison look weaker than it is. Option C matches each score to the same constant sixty, which produces differences that are just the scores shifted, so the pairing buys nothing. Option D spends the sample on a split that answers a different question and halves the precision of the answer actually wanted.
questions.hint: Ask whether the comparison value could have come out differently if it were measured again.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The correlation a paired design assumes
questions.learningObjective: explain how within-person correlation distorts a pre-post comparison
questions.stem: A pre-post study finds a statistically significant drop from pre-test to post-test and reports it as evidence that the training harmed performance. Which feature of the design makes that reading unsafe?

options.text: The same person supplied both scores, so the drop includes whatever the two scores of one person share regardless of the training
The pre-test was measured before the manipulation, so it cannot possibly have been affected by it
options.misconception: treats the timing of the measurement as settling the causal question

options.text: The two scores are not independent, so the analysis should have used an unpaired test rather than the paired test it used
options.misconception: turns non-independence into an argument against pairing rather than for it

options.text: The sample was not randomised, so the drop may be regression to the mean and the design proves nothing
options.misconception: names a genuine threat but stops short of the feature that applies to every study of this shape

questions.explanation: Two measurements from the same person carry that person's own level, and a strong pre-post correlation means a high scorer tends to stay high, so part of any drop is a property of the pairing rather than of the training, and only a control group on the same schedule can separate the two. Option B is true and irrelevant, since almost every design measures something first. Option C has the logic backwards, because the dependence is precisely what a paired analysis exists to handle, and handling it is what isolates the change. Option D names a real possibility that would apply to any design, including a well-controlled one, so it does not explain what is wrong with this comparison.
questions.hint: Ask what a person who scores high before the training would look like afterwards even if it did nothing.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Conditions for a test on one proportion
questions.learningObjective: identify the condition a small-count test on a proportion breaks
questions.stem: A clinic finds that 12 of 300 patients improved on a therapy, and a colleague proposes to repeat the comparison next year in a clinic expecting about 40 patients. Which condition of the usual test on a single proportion is most at risk?

options.text: The count of successes is small enough that a normal approximation to the binomial is unreliable, and 40 patients makes that worse
The benchmark must be exactly zero for a test on a single proportion, so any other reference value is inadmissible
options.misconception: insists on a null value that the test never required

options.text: The approximation needs at least ten observations in each of two groups, which a single proportion does not have
options.misconception: restates the condition as a requirement about a comparison the test does not make

options.text: Proportions from a clinic cannot be tested at all unless the patients were assigned to the therapy at random
options.misconception: confuses a test on observed proportions with a causal comparison between groups

questions.explanation: The usual test on one proportion leans on a normal approximation, which needs enough expected successes and enough expected non-successes for the approximation to behave, and a clinic expecting forty patients is going to produce even fewer of the rare outcome than the current clinic did. Option B mistakes the reference value the team supplies for a fixed requirement, when any proportion can serve as the value tested against. Option C imports a two-group condition into a one-sample procedure. Option D is about causal attribution rather than about whether a proportion can be summarised and tested at all, and random assignment bears on the first question, not the second.
questions.hint: Ask how many rare events the smaller clinic is likely to produce.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Expected counts in a chi-squared table
questions.learningObjective: compute an expected cell count from margins and state why it is the check
questions.stem: A two-by-two table crosses passing with attending a workshop. Of 90 attenders 30 passed, and of 60 non-attenders 30 passed. A reader wants the expected count for the attenders who passed. Which figure is it, and what is it for?

options.text: 36, from the row and column margins, and each expected count must be far enough above one or two for the test to be trusted
30, being the smallest observed count in its row and column, and it clears the usual minimum comfortably
options.misconception: takes an observed cell and calls it the expected one

options.text: 18, from applying the two group proportions to the total, and it is well clear of the minimum of five
options.misconception: applies proportions twice and lands on a count that was never in the table

options.text: 60, being the larger of the two margins involved, and a margin of that size is safe by construction
options.misconception: takes a margin as though it were a cell expectation

questions.explanation: An expected count is what the cell would hold if passing and attending were unrelated, and it comes from the row total of 90 times the column total of 60 divided by the grand total of 150, which gives 36. That figure matters because the chi-squared approximation is unreliable when any expected cell is very small, so a table has to be inspected for expected counts rather than observed ones, and a large observed count can sit in a cell whose expectation is thin. Options B, C and D each substitute a number that is present somewhere in the table for the one the calculation produces.
questions.hint: Ask what the cell would contain if the two variables were unrelated, and work from the margins.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a confidence interval licenses a writer to say
questions.learningObjective: identify the interpretation of an interval that survives scrutiny
questions.stem: A report states that it is 95 per cent confident that the mean repair delay lies between 4.2 and 6.8 seconds. Which reading of that sentence survives scrutiny?

options.text: The procedure that produced those bounds would capture the true mean in about 95 of every 100 repetitions on data like these, which is a claim about the method
There is a 95 per cent chance the true mean falls in this particular interval, now that the data are in hand
options.misconception: assigns a probability to the fixed parameter after conditioning on the data

options.text: The true mean is 5.5 seconds, and the interval simply records the uncertainty in that single number
options.misconception: treats the midpoint as the finding and the bounds as decoration

options.text: Ninety-five per cent of individual repair delays fall between 4.2 and 6.8 seconds
options.misconception: converts a statement about means into a statement about individual values

questions.explanation: The confidence level describes how often the procedure covers the truth, so it is a property of the method that can be checked by repeating the study, not a property of the particular interval now sitting in the report. Option B is the everyday reading and it is the one that does not survive, because once the data are fixed the mean is either in the interval or it is not, and no probability hangs on it. Option C mistakes the midpoint for a conclusion, and option D swaps the mean for the spread of individual observations, which is a much wider quantity that the interval was never estimating.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be repeated to check the 95 per cent.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a power calculation returns
questions.learningObjective: interpret the output of a sample size calculation for a planned test
questions.stem: A team runs a calculation for a two-sided comparison at five per cent with eighty per cent power to detect a difference of 0.3 standard deviations, and the calculation returns 64. They recruit 96 instead. What do the extra 32 buy?

options.text: Nothing for precision, because the calculation fixed the size at which the study has the stated chance of catching an effect of the stated size, and precision was never an input
Higher power against effects smaller than the one assumed, since power rises for every effect size once the sample grows
options.misconception: assumes one stated power applies to all effect sizes at once

options.text: A narrower interval for the same effect, because eighty per cent was also the target precision the calculation set
options.misconception: reads a power target as though it were a precision target

options.text: Insurance against the assumed effect being wrong, which is the purpose a power calculation is designed to serve
options.misconception: believes the calculation hedges the unknown effect size rather than fixing one of them

questions.explanation: A power calculation answers one narrow question, which is how large the sample must be for the study to have the stated chance of detecting the stated difference, and every other quantity is an input to that answer rather than an output from it. Recruiting beyond the figure gives a study that exceeds its requirement, which is rarely harmful, but it does not quietly convert the calculation into a precision plan, because the width of the interval was never computed. Options B, C and D each attach a benefit that the calculation never priced, and option D is the most common, since the assumed effect size is exactly the number a power calculation cannot defend.
questions.hint: Ask which quantities went into the calculation, and notice that precision is not one of them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: One-sample t statistic against a benchmark
questions.learningObjective: compute a one-sample t statistic from a sample mean, spread and size
questions.stem: A laboratory checks a new coating against a historical drying benchmark. Twenty samples dried in a mean of 72.4 minutes with a standard deviation of 10.2 minutes, and the benchmark is 70.0 minutes. Compute the one-sample t statistic for the comparison with that benchmark, giving the value to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The statistic is the observed difference from the benchmark divided by the standard error of the sample mean, and the standard error is the sample standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size, which here is 10.2 over 5, or 2.04 minutes. The observed difference is 2.4 minutes, so 2.4 over 2.04 gives 1.176. Dividing by the standard deviation rather than by its standard error would give 0.235, a figure a fifth of the size, and the tell for that error is that it would make a twenty-participant study look as precise as a two-hundred-participant one.
questions.hint: The standard error of a mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Standard error of a single proportion
questions.learningObjective: compute the standard error of an observed proportion
questions.stem: In a survey of 400 patients, 248 report that they had read the discharge summary before leaving the ward. Compute the standard error of the observed proportion, giving the value to four decimal places.
questions.explanation: The standard error of a proportion is the square root of the product of the proportion and its complement divided by the sample size, and 248 out of 400 is 0.62, whose complement is 0.38. Multiplying gives 0.2356 and dividing by 400 gives 0.000589, whose square root is 0.0243. A student who divides 0.62 by 400 obtains 0.00155 and then overstates precision by a factor of sixteen, and a student who uses 0.5 as the proportion because it is the value that maximises the product gets 0.025, which is close enough to be accepted by a careless marker and is wrong for these data.
questions.hint: Square root of the proportion times its complement, divided by the sample size.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chi-squared statistic from a small table
questions.learningObjective: sum the squared deviations from expectation across all four cells
questions.stem: A workshop table has 90 attenders of whom 30 passed, and 60 non-attenders of whom 30 passed, giving 150 people in total. Compute the chi-squared statistic by summing, over all four cells, the squared difference between the observed and expected counts divided by the expected count. Give the value to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The four expected counts come from the margins and total 150, giving 36, 54, 24 and 36, and the squared deviations from the observed 30, 60, 30 and 30 are 36 in every cell. Dividing each by its own expected count and adding gives 1.000 for the first cell, 0.667 for the second, 1.500 for the third and 1.000 for the fourth, which sums to 4.167. The error that looks most reasonable is to divide all four deviations by a single expected count, which would give 4.000, and it is wrong because the cell with the smallest expectation contributes the most.
questions.hint: Each cell contributes its own squared deviation divided by its own expected count.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Sample size from a calculation for a proportion
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a stated sample size formula for a proportion and round it up
questions.stem: A team plans a two-sided test at the five per cent level with eighty per cent power to detect a difference of 0.25 in a proportion expected to be 0.5, using the formula n = (1.96 + 0.84) squared times 0.5 times 0.5 divided by 0.25 squared. Compute n and report the value rounded up to the next whole participant.
questions.explanation: The two normal values are 1.96 for the two-sided five per cent level and 0.84 for eighty per cent power, and they add to 2.80, whose square is 7.84. The variance term 0.5 times 0.5 is 0.25, so the numerator is 1.96, and the squared effect size is 0.0625, giving 31.36 participants. A sample is rounded up rather than down, because 31 would leave the study slightly under the requested power, so 32 is the answer. Rounding to 31 looks tidy and quietly buys less power than the plan claimed, and using 0.84 for the whole test would give a noticeably smaller and underpowered sample.
questions.hint: Add the two normal values, square the sum, then divide the variance term by the squared effect size.

questions.topic: Adjusted R-squared for models of different size
questions.learningObjective: compute an adjusted R-squared and state what the adjustment penalises
questions.stem: A model fitted to 50 observations with two predictors explains 40 per cent of the variance in the outcome. Compute the adjusted R-squared using the formula 1 minus (1 minus the R-squared) times 49 divided by 47, and give the value to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Substituting gives 1 minus 0.6 times 49 over 47, and 0.6 times 49 is 29.4, which divided by 47 is 0.6255, so the adjusted figure is 0.374. It sits below the plain 0.400 because the adjustment charges the model for the two predictors it spent, and with fifty observations that charge is real rather than trivial. A student who divides by 48 instead of 47 gets 0.388, close enough to look like rounding, and a student who forgets to multiply the shortfall by 49 gets 0.987, which is the value that appears when the degrees of freedom are read as though the sample were enormous.

questions.topic: A t test justified by a large sample alone
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a test choice that leans on sample size to excuse a violated assumption
questions.stem: A report compares a treatment group of 200 with a control group of 200. The outcome is strongly right-skewed in the control group and the two groups' standard deviations differ by a factor of three. The analysis uses a pooled-variance t test and the text says only that the sample is large. Which statement describes the situation accurately?

options.text: The large sample makes the mean comparison approximately valid but leaves the threefold spread difference as a separate problem, since the pooled estimate describes neither group well
The large sample makes the pooled estimate valid, because the approximation applies to the spread as well as to the mean
options.misconception: extends an approximation about means to a quantity it says nothing about

options.text: The spread difference is the reason the analysis failed, since a pooled estimate is only computed when the spreads match exactly
options.misconception: demands an exact match rather than a workable approximation

options.text: Neither feature is a problem at this sample size, because two hundred observations per group removes distributional concerns
options.misconception: treats sample size as a cure for every assumption the test has

questions.explanation: Two hundred per group is enough for the mean of each group to behave approximately normally even with skew in the raw values, so the size of the sample genuinely does settle one of the two assumptions. It settles nothing about the spread, and when the groups differ threefold the pooled standard deviation is a compromise that describes neither one, which is the situation that inflates the error rate beyond the nominal five per cent. questions.topic: A forecast presented without an interval
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a point forecast that hides the uncertainty a decision would need
questions.stem: A demand model issues a forecast of 1,240 units for next quarter as a single number, and the operations team will order to that figure. Which statement identifies what the model has left out?

options.text: The spread of outcomes around the figure, since an order placed at the central value is wrong a known fraction of the time and the fraction is unknown here

options.text: The residual error from the training data, since that figure would let the team widen its own order by judgement
options.misconception: suggests a quantity the team would have to reinterpret rather than one it could use

options.text: The confidence of the analysts who built the model, since an interval can only be produced by experienced modellers

questions.topic: A prediction interval against an interval around a mean
questions.learningObjective: explain why a forecast needs a wider interval than a fitted mean
questions.stem: A fitted line gives an interval around each estimated mean value, and a second, wider interval around what the next observation will be. Explain why the second interval is wider, and what each of the two is for.

answer.exemplar: The two intervals are answering different questions and that is the whole of the difference. The narrower one covers the average of many future observations at that point on the line, so it only has to account for the uncertainty in where the average sits, which is a quantity that shrinks as the data support the line more firmly. The wider one covers a single future observation, and a single observation carries everything the average does not, namely the ordinary scatter of individual cases about the line, and that scatter is a property of the process rather than of how much data has been collected. So a fitted mean with a tight interval can sit inside a forecast whose interval is many times wider, and the arithmetic difference between the two is the estimated spread of individual outcomes, which is why quoting the narrow interval for an individual forecast is a mistake that understates the spread by a factor of roughly the square root of the sample size, and that factor grows as the evidence accumulates.

questions.topic: Calibration and discrimination are different properties
questions.learningObjective: explain how a model can rank well while predicting the wrong rates
questions.stem: One risk model orders patients correctly from highest to lowest risk but assigns every patient the same number. Another assigns well-calibrated rates but orders patients almost at random. Explain how each can be true at once, and why a service needs both.

answer.exemplar: The two properties are separable because they are answers to two different questions, and separating them is the useful part of the idea. Discrimination asks whether the ordering of the scores matches the ordering of the outcomes, and it is a property of the ranking alone, so a model that outputs a single constant ranks every patient identically and therefore discriminates not at all, whatever else it may be doing well. Calibration asks whether the numbers themselves are right, so a model that predicts ten per cent risk where the observed rate is ten per cent, and sixty where it is sixty, is perfectly calibrated while the spread of its predictions may be far too small to order anyone. A constant prediction is the extreme case, and it can be perfectly calibrated and perfectly undiscriminating at the same time. This is why a service cannot pick one property to optimise: ordering decides who is seen first, and only the numbers decide whether a risk conversation with a patient is honest, so a model that is wrong about who is at highest risk sends attention to the wrong people, and a model that is right about the ordering while wrong about the levels tells a patient a probability that is not theirs.

questions.explanation: A strong response treats the two as answers to different questions, notes that a constant prediction is well calibrated and undiscriminating, and explains why a service needs ordering for triage and correct levels for honest communication.
questions.hint: Ask what a model would be doing if it gave every patient the same number.

questions.stem: A service knows that a missed sepsis case costs far more than a false alarm. Explain what that knowledge should change about the model, what it should not change, and why.

answer.exemplar: The knowledge is about consequences, and the ranking of patients by risk is a statement about the world, so the costs belong in the decision rule and not in the model. A model that ranks a patient above another has made a claim that can be checked against outcomes, and no information about hospital costs changes whether that claim is true, so refitting the model to weight expensive mistakes more heavily produces a worse estimate in exchange for a better policy. What the costs legitimately move is the point at which the service acts, and the further they favour catching cases the lower that cut-off goes, with the number of false alarms and the work they create rising to pay for it. The trap is that a service which has been burned by a false alarm wants a model that produces fewer of them, and the only honest way to get that is to improve the model's ability to separate the two groups, not to raise the bar until the alarm rate looks acceptable. So the cost matrix is an argument for a different threshold and a better instrument, and never an argument for a model that has been tuned to make a chosen number look good.

questions.explanation: A strong response separates the model from the decision rule, explains that costs legitimately move the cut-off while leaving the ranking alone, and identifies model improvement as the only honest route to fewer false alarms.

questions.learningObjective: sequence the transformations that make a series usable for modelling
questions.stem: A monthly series of 96 observations has to be made ready for modelling. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Plot the series in time order with the scale visible, so any trend and any repeating pattern can be seen
Take first differences to remove the level drift, then plot them and check what is left
Examine the autocorrelation of the differenced series to find which lags still carry structure
Estimate and remove the seasonal pattern the autocorrelation revealed, rather than assuming its length
Record each transformation and the order it was applied in, so the series can be rebuilt as found

questions.explanation: Nothing is transformed before the series has been looked at, because the plot is what tells the analyst whether there is a drift to remove and a cycle to look for, and a transformation chosen in advance of the plot is a transformation chosen blind. The first differences then remove the level drift, and plotting them shows what the drift was hiding. The autocorrelation of the differenced series is examined before any seasonal model is chosen, so the cycle's length is read off the data rather than assumed to be twelve, and a spike at a lag that is not twelve is exactly the sort of thing the plot would have made obvious and the assumption would have missed. The seasonal part is removed once its length is established, and the record of what was done in what order is what allows the series to be put back the way it was found, which is the difference between a transformation and an irreversible edit.
questions.hint: Look before transforming, and let the diagnostics set the length of the cycle.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: An effect size read against a field's benchmarks
questions.learningObjective: judge a reported effect size against the reference points its field supplies
questions.stem: Two studies both clear a significance threshold. One reports a standardised difference of 0.12 in an area with no agreed benchmarks, the other 0.80 where published benchmarks exist. Which statement is the defensible reading?

options.text: The 0.80 can be set against its field's benchmarks and judged, while the 0.12 has no reference beyond the word small, which is the reporting team's own choice
The 0.12 matters more, since it cleared the same significance threshold that the 0.80 cleared
options.misconception: treats a shared decision rule as though it made two magnitudes comparable

options.text: The 0.80 is the more suspicious result, since an effect of that size usually signals a design problem rather than a real finding
options.misconception: treats a large estimate as evidence of a fault without naming one

options.text: Both can be judged, because a fixed dividing line between small and medium is used across every field
options.misconception: assumes one set of labels travels between fields whose outcomes do not

questions.explanation: An effect size becomes interpretable when it can be set against something, and what counts as something is decided by the field, since a standardised difference of 0.8 in a reaction time and one of 0.8 in a survival outcome are not the same size of event at all. Where no benchmark exists the number is still worth reporting but not worth ranking, and saying small about it is a judgement about wording rather than about magnitude. Option B shows what significance does, which is to flatten magnitudes into a decision. Option C is a suspicion without a diagnosis. Option D imports one field's labels into another, which is the error that makes cross-disciplinary comparisons fail.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would compare each number against.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: One coefficient in a model with several predictors
questions.learningObjective: interpret a single regression coefficient with the other predictors held
questions.stem: A model predicts a score from hours of practice, prior attainment and a motivational instruction. The instruction's coefficient is 2.1 with an interval from 0.4 to 3.8. Which statement is the right reading?

options.text: With prior attainment and practice held at their observed values, the instruction is associated with about two more points, and the interval allows the association to be smaller than a point
The instruction raises the score by 2.1 points on average, since a coefficient becomes a causal effect once it has been estimated
options.misconception: turns a held-comparison association into an intervention effect the design did not perform

options.text: The instruction raises the score by 2.1 points for each extra hour of practice, since a coefficient is read per unit of the model
options.misconception: reads a coefficient as if it were attached to a different predictor

options.text: The instruction has no measurable effect, since its interval runs from 0.4 rather than from 0
options.misconception: treats a specific bound as though significance required the interval to contain zero

questions.explanation: In a model with several predictors each coefficient answers a comparison in which the others are held where they are, so 2.1 is the difference in score associated with the instruction at a given level of practice and prior attainment, and the interval says the data are compatible with that difference being as small as 0.4. Option B drops the comparison and asserts a cause, which the design must earn. Option C attaches the number to the wrong predictor, which is the error that makes a multiple regression look like a statement about everything at once. Option D inverts the significance logic, since an interval clear of zero is exactly the case where a difference is supported.
questions.hint: Ask what the coefficient holds constant, and which comparison it is one part of.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What an interaction term does to a main effect
questions.learningObjective: explain how a product term changes the meaning of the two main coefficients
questions.stem: A model of training hours and practice method, with a product term, reports 6 points per hour under the usual method and 2 points per hour under the new one. Which statement explains what the product term changed?

options.text: It made the effect of training depend on the method, so the method's effect is no longer one number and varies with how much training a learner gets
It added another predictor, so the smaller figure shows the new method is worse at every level of training
options.misconception: reads a conditional slope as though it applied everywhere

options.text: It tested whether the two main effects are individually significant, which is what the two coefficients report
options.misconception: attributes a separate test to a term that changes the model rather than checks it

options.text: It averaged the two slopes into one, which is why the report gives two different numbers
options.misconception: describes a collapse as though the two numbers were the result of it

questions.explanation: Once a product term is present the two coefficients are no longer statements about each predictor on its own but statements about the effect of one at a reference value of the other, so 6 is the slope of training where the method is at its reference value and 2 is the slope at one unit of the method, and the difference between the two is itself a coefficient the model has estimated. Option B reads a conditional slope as though it were general, which is the misreading the interaction is built to prevent. Option C mistakes a term that changes the model for a test of its parts. Option D has the direction backwards, since the interaction is what keeps the two slopes apart rather than merging them.
questions.hint: Ask what the slope of one predictor is at a particular level of the other.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The shape a squared term fits
questions.learningObjective: match a curved pattern to the term that can represent it
questions.stem: Study hours run against score. The points climb steeply at first and then flatten near the top of the scale. Which change fits that shape, and why?

options.text: Add a squared term, because the relationship bends and a squared term lets the fitted curve turn over instead of holding one slope across the whole range
Add a fourth-order term, because a curve that flattens can only be captured by a very high order of the predictor
options.misconception: believes more flexibility always buys a better description of a simple bend

options.text: Split the scores into bands and fit one mean per band, because a curved relationship must be handled by grouping the outcome
options.misconception: replaces a smooth curve with a step function and discards the ordering inside each band

options.text: Add a product term with the score ceiling, because the flattening is caused by the instrument rather than by the relationship
options.misconception: attributes the shape to the measure and models the interaction instead of the curve

questions.explanation: A squared term is the smallest change that lets a fitted line bend, and a pattern that climbs then flattens is the shape it produces, with the model free to estimate where the turning point sits rather than having it imposed. Option B reaches for flexibility instead of for fit, and a fourth-order term fitted to a single bend will chase the points as well as the curve. Option C throws away the information that the score is ordered, replacing a relationship with a set of group means. Option D assumes the instrument causes the shape, which would need evidence of its own, and even then a product with a ceiling does not bend the fitted line.
questions.hint: Ask what the smallest change is that lets the fitted line change direction.

questions.topic: What a logged response does to a coefficient
questions.learningObjective: state the change a log response makes to what a coefficient licenses
questions.stem: A regression of the logarithm of annual income on years of schooling gives a coefficient of 0.06. Which statement describes what that number licenses the writer to say?

options.text: Each additional year of schooling goes with about 6 per cent higher income, because a unit rise in a logged response is a constant percentage rather than a constant amount
Each additional year raises income by 6 percentage points, because a coefficient is read in the units of the response
options.misconception: reads a percentage as though it were a percentage-point shift

options.text: Each additional year raises income by six currency units, because the transformation only relabels the axis
options.misconception: assumes a transformation that changes the scale also leaves the coefficient in the old units

options.text: Each additional year changes income by 0.06 units on the original scale, so nothing is gained by logging the outcome at all
options.misconception: reports the coefficient as though it were already on the original scale

questions.explanation: A logarithm turns a constant amount into a constant percentage, so a coefficient of 0.06 on a logged outcome describes a 6 per cent change per unit of the predictor, and a 1.06 factor rather than an addition of six. Option B confuses a relative change with a change in percentage points, which is the error that makes income and attainment look comparable to a percentage of an exam mark. Option C is the belief that logging relabels rather than rescales, and it produces a number in currency units that nobody fitted. Option D reports the fitted value as though it were an original-scale one, which discards the whole reason for taking the logarithm.
questions.hint: Ask what a constant step on the logged scale means on the original one.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Leakage in a backtest
questions.learningObjective: identify information from the future that has entered a historical test
questions.stem: A model is backtested over two years, and the reported accuracy is 91 per cent. The inputs were rescaled and the missing values filled using statistics computed across the whole two-year period before the data were split into earlier and later halves. Which statement is the accurate diagnosis?

options.text: The summaries used to prepare the inputs already contain the later period, so the model is partly predicting from information it would not have had at the time
Rescaling and filling are preparation steps that carry no information about outcomes, so the split still tests the method honestly
options.misconception: believes data preparation cannot carry outcome information

options.text: The accuracy is inflated only because the two halves overlap, and the fix is to shift the split boundary forward one day
options.misconception: attaches the inflation to overlap rather than to the summaries used

options.text: The backtest is sound because the model was never shown the later outcomes during fitting, and preparation is not fitting
options.misconception: confuses withholding labels with withholding information about the cases

questions.explanation: A backtest is a claim that the method could have been run at the time, and that claim fails the moment any step of preparation uses the whole period, because a mean or a fill computed over two years encodes the later period's distribution and the model can then recognise cases it has already been shaped by, which is why the reported accuracy exceeds what the method would have delivered in real time. Option B is the assumption the exercise exists to break. Option C names a real and separate fault, since overlapping windows leak too, and fixing it would not repair the preparation step. Option D is the distinction that makes the fault easy to miss, because labels were indeed withheld while information about the cases was not.
questions.hint: Ask whether every step could have been run with only the past available.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A conclusion its own residual plot contradicts
questions.learningObjective: read a claim against the diagnostic that fails to support it
questions.stem: A report concludes that dose rises linearly with response across the whole range. Its residual plot against dose shows a clear arc, with positives at both ends and negatives in the middle, and the report does not mention the plot. Which statement is the fair reading?

options.text: The plot shows the single straight line cannot represent the pattern, so the claim of one constant rate across the range is not supported by the paper's own diagnostic
The plot is uninformative, because residuals are supposed to average to zero and a visible arc is what that property looks like
options.misconception: treats the zero-sum property as a description of the shape rather than of the average

options.text: The claim is safe, because the fit is the best a straight line can do and no better shape is available
options.misconception: confuses the limit of the fitted form with the limit of the data

options.text: The plot settles the matter against the straight line, so the correct response is to report the diagnostic and drop the claim entirely
options.misconception: overcorrects from a mis-specified model to the loss of the relationship

questions.explanation: A residual plot exists to show whether the fitted form has absorbed the pattern, and an arc of positive residuals at the ends with negatives in the middle is the signature of a relationship that curves, so the model has left structure behind and the claim of one constant rate is contradicted by the paper's own figure. Option B mistakes a property of the average for a property of the shape. Option C confuses the best a straight line can achieve with the best any model can achieve, when a squared term is right there. Option D goes too far and discards a real relationship over a mis-specified model.
questions.hint: Ask what shape would leave the residuals positive at the ends and negative in the middle.

questions.topic: An average that hides the shape of the data
questions.learningObjective: identify what a single slope reports for a relationship that changes rate
questions.stem: A straight-line model is fitted to a series that rises quickly over the first third of the range and is flat over the last two thirds, and the report gives the slope as the effect of one more unit. Which statement describes the misreading this produces?

options.text: The single slope is an average pulled toward the crowded part of the range, so it overstates the gain at the flat end and understates it at the steep end
The slope is unbiased at every point, and the problem lies only in how its standard error was computed
options.misconception: claims pointwise accuracy for an average and misplaces the defect

options.text: No slope may be reported for a relationship that bends, so the figure should be withdrawn without replacement
options.misconception: rules out a summary that is merely qualified rather than wrong

options.text: The slope is unbiased but imprecise, so the only remedy is a larger sample and not a different model
options.misconception: prescribes more data for a problem that more data will not fix

questions.explanation: A single slope is one number standing for a relationship that changes rate, and where the data are crowded at the flat end that number is pulled toward the flat part, so it is a fair description of the average and a poor description of either end. Option B claims the average holds pointwise, which is exactly what an average of a changing quantity does not do. Option C is an overcorrection, since a summary of a bent relationship is legitimate once it is labelled as an average. Option D is the practical trap, because recruiting more points from the same flat range narrows the interval around a number that answers the wrong question.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the range the data crowd into, and which part they thin out.

questions.topic: A response transformed before it is modelled
questions.learningObjective: state what a transformation achieves and where the assumption is then judged
questions.stem: Minutes of waiting time for 200 appointments has a long right tail, and the team models the logarithm of waiting time rather than the minutes. Which statement is the accurate account of the change?

options.text: The tail is pulled in, so the residuals become closer to symmetric, and the model's assumptions are now judged on the logged scale and reported there
The observations in the tail are discarded, since a logarithm has no value for a wait several times the average
options.misconception: believes a transformation removes extreme cases

options.text: Differences on the logged scale are additive, so a difference of logs can be read directly as a difference in minutes
options.misconception: claims additivity that the transformation removes

options.text: The outcome has effectively changed, so any finding about the model no longer speaks about waiting time
options.misconception: treats a change of scale as a change of subject

questions.explanation: A logarithm compresses the far end of a long right tail far more than the middle, which is exactly what a model of a mean wants, and once the model is fitted on the logged scale its assumptions are assessed on the residuals of that scale and reported in those units. Option B is wrong because a logarithm is defined for every positive waiting time, however long, and the tail is squeezed rather than lost. Option C is the property the transformation takes away, since a constant difference in logarithms is a constant ratio and not a constant number of minutes. Option D confuses a change of units with a change of what is being measured.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a value many times the average, and whether it is still there afterwards.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What the adjusted R-squared correction is for
questions.learningObjective: explain why models of different size cannot be compared on plain R-squared
questions.stem: A team fits a three-predictor model, then a five-predictor model, and quotes the second as the better one because its R-squared is higher. Explain why that comparison is not available, what the adjusted figure changes, and what the comparison still cannot settle.

answer.exemplar: Plain R-squared cannot support the comparison because it is a share of the variation the model accounts for and no such share is charged for the predictors spent on accounting for it, so adding a fifth predictor to a three-predictor model cannot reduce the figure and usually raises it, and a model that has captured the true structure with two predictors will be beaten by a model with five that has captured it with the same two plus three spurious ones. The adjusted figure charges the model for what it spent, by scaling the unexplained part by the ratio of residual to total degrees of freedom, so a predictor now has to earn its place before it can improve the number, which is what makes the comparison legitimate rather than automatic. What the adjustment still cannot settle is which model a reader should believe, because both the penalty and the estimate are computed on the same data that chose the predictors, and a term included because it was significant on that data will usually look worth including a second time. So the adjusted figure is what permits the ranking to be made at all, and it is not evidence that the winner is right, which is why a serious report also asks whether the two models would be ranked the same way on data neither has seen.

questions.explanation: A strong response says plain R-squared never falls when a predictor is added, explains that the adjustment charges for predictors spent, and notes that the winner may still be an artefact of choosing predictors on the same data.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the plain figure when a fifth predictor is added.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a multicollinearity diagnostic matters even without a fault
questions.learningObjective: explain what shared variance does to coefficient stability without making a predictor useless
questions.stem: Two predictors correlate at 0.8, giving each a variance inflation factor near 2.8, and their separate coefficients move about a twentieth when a third variable is added. Explain what is wrong and what is not.

answer.exemplar: Nothing is wrong with the model and something is wrong with the precision of the reading, and separating those two sentences is the whole of the point. The two predictors share the variance they each carry, so the model cannot decide how much of an outcome belongs to one and how much to the other, and when a third variable shifts a little of the shared part from one to the other, both coefficients move while the prediction barely changes at all. The prediction is the thing the model was built for and it has survived intact, which is why a team may reasonably go on using the model for prediction. What has not survived is the ability to say anything about one predictor on its own, since a coefficient of 2.1 with an interval wide enough to cross zero is a statement about a quantity the data never pinned down. A variance inflation factor near 2.8 is also not a diagnosis of catastrophe, since the alarms are usually reserved for values several times higher, and a factor in this range is the ordinary cost of measuring two related things. The right response is to report the overlap, to avoid interpreting either coefficient on its own, and to prefer the more directly measured of the two where a decision requires one, rather than to delete a predictor that has earned its place.

questions.explanation: A strong response separates the stability of predictions from the interpretability of individual coefficients, and reads a factor near 2.8 as an ordinary cost rather than a failure.
questions.hint: Ask whether the model's predictions moved as much as the coefficients did.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a rank-based test buys and gives up
questions.learningObjective: explain the exchange made when a parametric test is replaced by a rank-based one
questions.stem: A team replaces a t test on the differences with a signed-rank procedure because the differences are heavily tied. Explain what the replacement makes safe, what it stops the team from saying, and why the choice is a trade rather than an improvement.

answer.exemplar: The replacement makes safe the one thing the original test could not promise, which is that its approximation rests on the order of the differences rather than on their shape, and a difference distribution full of ties and a long upper tail is exactly where that promise is worth having. What it stops the team from saying is a matter of units. A t test produces a difference in the original measurement, so a reader learns how many points, days or units separated the two conditions, and a signed-rank procedure produces a comparison of ranks, which is a statement about how the differences are ordered and not about how large they were, so the number that comes out cannot be translated into the quantity a decision would be taken on. That is not a small loss, and it is also not a defect of the method, because the method is not claiming to supply units. What makes this a trade rather than an improvement is that the two procedures are answering the same question at different levels of resolution, and the choice of which question to ask is a decision about what the study needs to say, not a piece of statistical housekeeping that a careful analyst can make on the team's behalf by picking the procedure with the weaker assumption.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the rank-based test rests on order rather than shape, that its result cannot be translated into original units, and that the choice is a decision about which question the study needs answered.
questions.hint: Ask what unit the answer comes in, and whether the original test could give one.

questions.topic: Reading a curve and specifying the model that fits it
questions.learningObjective: move from a pattern in the data to a model that can represent it
questions.stem: A scatter of score against revision hours curves upward and then levels off, and a straight line has been fitted. First say what the shape tells you about the line, then say what the next model has to be able to do.

options.text: The line has to hold one slope where the relationship changes rate, so the next model has to be able to bend, most simply by adding a squared term
The line is right, because the points lie on both sides of it and a well-fitted line always has residuals on both sides
options.misconception: takes residual spread as evidence that the form is adequate

options.text: The points are too scattered to model, so the next step is to collect more observations before fitting anything else
options.misconception: treats scatter as though it were the problem rather than the form

options.text: The line should be fitted to the logs of both variables, because a curve on the original scale is always a line on a log scale
options.misconception: prescribes a particular remedy as though curves had only one possible cause

Here they will run positive at one end, negative through the middle and positive at the other, and the model that can reproduce that is one whose fitted value is free to change slope, which a squared term provides. Option B mistakes a defining property for a diagnostic. Option C proposes more data where a change of form would do. Option D names one possible source of curvature as though it were the only one, and a curve that flattens is not what a straight line becomes on a log scale.
questions.hint: Ask what the residuals look like, not whether they straddle the line.

questions.topic: Comparing two models of different size
questions.learningObjective: state what must be held comparable before two models can be ranked

It shows the extra two predictors explained a real part of the outcome, and it does not show how large that part is in original units
options.misconception: reads an increase in accounted variation as evidence of a real contribution

options.text: It shows the four-predictor model is better, and it does not show the two-predictor model would not be better still on other data
options.misconception: names the ranking as settled when the ranking is what is in question

options.text: It shows nothing at all, since R-squared is not defined for models with a different number of predictors
options.misconception: believes the figure is unavailable rather than uninformative

The comparison becomes available only once the fit is charged for the predictors it spent, and even then the winner is a winner on these records, since both the penalty and the coefficients were computed on the data that chose the predictors. questions.topic: A stated conclusion and the diagnostic that opposes it
questions.learningObjective: weigh a stated claim against the diagnostic that fails to support it

options.text: The claim is that both predictors matter, and the inflation factor shows the smaller coefficient should be dropped from the model

Option D asserts the redundancy the factor is being used to characterise rather than to confirm.

questions.learningObjective: sequence a transformation from diagnosis to the units the result will be reported in
questions.stem: A response is strongly right-skewed with a long tail, and the team will model it after transforming it. First say what the team must establish before choosing the transformation, then say what they will have to remember when they report the result.

options.text: That the outliers have been removed first, and that the coefficient is then a statement about the trimmed sample alone
options.misconception: supplies a data edit the question never proposed

questions.topic: From a research question to a chosen test
questions.learningObjective: sequence the reasoning that connects a question to a statistical test
questions.stem: A team must choose a test before it collects data. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Write down the comparison in terms of measured variables, saying what differs and what is held the same
Decide how many groups or measurements the comparison involves and whether they come from the same people
Check the shape of the outcome, since it decides which distributional assumption is even available to test
Name the test whose assumptions are met and say which one would be used instead if the shape ruled it out
Fix the benchmark or the null value the comparison will be judged against, since the test does not supply one

questions.explanation: The comparison is written first, in the language of the measures rather than of the test, because a test chosen before anyone has said what is being compared will be chosen for its reputation rather than for the question, and several perfectly good tests can serve one comparison and only one can serve another. The structure of the comparison comes next, since whether there are two independent groups, one group against a benchmark or two measurements from the same people decides the whole family of tests that is even available. The shape of the outcome is examined before any test is named, because it determines which assumption can be met and a test chosen in advance of that check is a test chosen on hope. The test is then named together with its fallback, since a team that has said what it will do when the shape rules out the preferred test has also protected itself from choosing afterwards, and only when all of that is settled is the benchmark fixed, because the value a result will be judged against is a decision about the question and not something the arithmetic can supply.
questions.hint: Decide what is being compared before naming anything that computes it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: From a fitted model to a table a reader can check
questions.learningObjective: sequence the assembly of a checkable display from a completed analysis
questions.stem: An analysis is complete and a table is to be built from it. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Fix the sample and the definitions each column will use, so two figures are not built on different cases
Compute the count behind every percentage, so each share has a denominator beside it
Compute the comparison and its interval, in the units the outcome is measured in
Add the spread within each group, since two means with no spread cannot be told apart from two identical means
Write the caption saying what the reader is looking at and which rows were excluded, if any

questions.explanation: The sample and the definitions are fixed before any number is produced, because two columns computed on different cases will agree or disagree for reasons no reader can see, and a definition that changes between columns is a difference in the table that no amount of careful arithmetic afterwards will explain. Counts are computed before shares so that every percentage arrives with the number it multiplies, which is the one omission that makes a table impossible to check. The comparison and its interval come next and in the outcome's own units, because a reader who has to convert before they can interpret will not convert. The spread within each group is added because a table of means is a table that conceals the difference between two groups that are genuinely alike and two groups where every case in one sits above every case in the other, and the caption is written last so that it can say what the table actually contains, including any rows that were left out and why.
questions.hint: Fix what the columns will be before computing anything that fills them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: An interval read against a benchmark and a threshold
questions.learningObjective: interpret an interval that excludes a null but not a practical threshold
questions.stem: A comparison of two methods gives a difference of 4.0 units with an interval from 0.2 to 7.8, and the report says the difference is established. What is the fair reading?

options.text: A difference from zero is supported because the interval excludes it, while the low end leaves room for an effect too small to be worth acting on, so established is doing more work than the interval allows
The difference is established, since an interval excluding zero settles the question and any threshold is a matter for somebody else
options.misconception: confuses a decision about zero with a decision about a practical threshold

options.text: The difference is not established, since the interval runs from 0.2 and an interval must contain zero to be inclusive
options.misconception: inverts the significance rule and reads a bound as though it were a null

options.text: The difference is established for the average case only, since an interval describes means and says nothing about individual results
options.misconception: correctly notes the target of the interval and then uses it to dismiss the finding

questions.explanation: The interval does two jobs at once, and here they point in different directions: it excludes zero, so the data are hard to reconcile with no difference at all, and it reaches down to 0.2, so the data are also compatible with a difference so small that nobody would change anything for it. A report that says only that the difference is established has reported the half of the interval that supports it and dropped the half that a decision-maker needs, and the fix is not a different analysis but a sentence naming the threshold and saying where the interval sits relative to it. Option B accepts the division of labour that produces the omission. Option C inverts the significance rule. Option D notes correctly that the interval concerns averages and then uses that fact to dismiss a finding about averages.
questions.hint: Ask two questions of the interval, one about zero and one about the smallest useful effect.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A coefficient whose interval covers both directions
questions.learningObjective: interpret a summary sentence that claims more than the intervals support
questions.stem: A model reports two predictors. The first has a coefficient of 0.8 with an interval from 0.1 to 1.5. The second has a coefficient of -0.4 with an interval from -1.2 to 0.4. The report's summary says the first raises the outcome and the second lowers it. What is the fair reading?

options.text: The direction of the first is supported and the direction of the second is not, so a sentence that names both as established asserts for the second something its own interval leaves open
Both are established, since a coefficient carries its own direction regardless of how wide the interval around it is
options.misconception: ignores the interval entirely and treats the estimate as the finding

options.text: Neither is established, because a model with more than one predictor only supports conclusions about the model as a whole
options.misconception: denies that any individual coefficient can be supported

options.text: Both are established, since the two intervals overlap and overlapping intervals cannot contradict each other
options.misconception: reads an overlap as mutual confirmation of two separate claims

questions.explanation: The first interval lies wholly above zero, so the sign of that estimate is supported, while the second runs from a value that would raise the outcome to a value that would lower it, and a quantity the data leave straddling zero has no established direction at all. The summary sentence has taken both central estimates at face value and reported them with equal confidence, and that is a different claim from the one the intervals support, and it is a claim a reader is likely to act on. Option B is the plainest form of the error, treating a point estimate as a finding. Option C is an overcorrection that would leave nothing interpretable in any model. Option D is confused about what overlapping intervals say, which is that neither settles the other, not that both are settled.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two intervals stays on one side of zero.
